Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Patients with depressive disorder had decreased vitamin D levels compared with healthy controls.
Sentence: "The patients with DD had elevated TXB levels and decreased vitamin D levels, as compared to healthy controls."
Measured as: depressive disorder (vs healthy controls)
Population: Children and adolescents with depressive disorder and healthy controls
Intervention: Baseline vitamin D level (observational comparison)
Comparator: Healthy controls
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 58
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Dietary vitamin D intake was not significantly associated with risk of depression in the fully adjusted model.
Sentence: "No significant association was found between vitamin D dietary intake and risk of depression in the full-adjusted model (OR: 0.96, 95% CI: 0.62, 1.51)."
Measured as: risk of depression (Beck Depression Inventory-II)
Population: 690 healthy physically active adults (athletes) aged 18-50 in Kashan, Iran
Intervention: Dietary vitamin D intake assessed by 147-item FFQ (tertiles)
Comparator: Lowest tertile of vitamin D intake
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 690
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Study A is a study of baseline vitamin D levels in children, while Study B is a cross-sectional study of dietary intake in adult athletes; the exposure measures differ in population and design.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"population","also_differs":["design_or_bias","outcome_measure"],"detail":"population: children/adolescents with depressive disorder vs 690 physically active adults aged 18-50; design: RCT label for an observational level comparison vs cross-sectional dietary intake study"}
